finding.claim: Mass assignment on PUT /me: the entire request body is merged into the authenticated user object and persisted. An authenticated low-privilege user can set arbitrary fields such as role, isAdmin, id, email, or tenant/org id, giving privilege escalation or account takeover. Inherited prototype keys are not a concern because Object.assign copies own enumerable properties only, but a JSON body with a __proto__ key is an own property and is assigned via the setter on the target.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled req.body JSON on PUT /me (any authenticated user)
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) followed by req.store.save(req.user), which persists the modified user record

trace.note: PUT /me handler registered with no field allowlist or role check
Object.assign(req.user, req.body) copies all attacker-supplied keys onto the user record
The full modified user is returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: Only users.js exists in the directory. It has no body validation, no field allowlist, and no schema. Any authentication middleware that populates req.user is not in the repo, so I could not check it. Even if it exists, it does not limit which fields the body may set. The sibling route PUT /me/profile (lines 10-15) destructures only displayName and bio, which shows the intended allowlist pattern and that /me bypasses it.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 runs Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist or validation, and users.js:6 persists it, while the sibling route at users.js:11-12 destructures only displayName and bio. Any authenticated user can therefore set role, isAdmin or similar fields. Any auth middleware is outside the repo, so it could not be checked, but it would not limit which body fields are accepted. The claim's mention of a __proto__ key adds nothing to the finding.
